title: Turning a superconducting diode into a Feynman ratchet to realize a nanoscale heat engine
authors: Konstantinos Kontogeorgiou, İnanç Adagideli, Géraldine Haack, Fabian Hassler
abstract: Feynman's ratchet illustrates how work can be extracted from thermal fluctuations in the presence of two heat baths at different temperatures. While some experimental realizations of the ratchet effect have been studied, most lack miniaturization, which is important for some applications. Here, we propose a physical implementation of Feynman's ratchet based on Josephson junctions exhibiting the superconducting diode effect. This setup functions as a heat engine that generates work solely from a temperature gradient via thermal fluctuations. We analyze its output power and efficiency, and, through the Seebeck coefficient, identify the conditions under which the device operates in reverse, functioning instead as a Peltier cooler.
summary: The authors propose using a superconducting diode as a physical realization of a Feynman ratchet to build a nanoscale heat engine. By exploiting thermal fluctuations across a temperature gradient, the device can generate directed work, demonstrating energy conversion efficiency. Furthermore, the analysis shows it can operate in reverse, functioning as a Peltier cooler.
main_problem: To realize a nanoscale heat engine by converting thermal energy into work using a superconducting diode acting as a Feynman ratchet.
main_result: The setup successfully functions as a heat engine, generating work from a temperature gradient via thermal fluctuations, and can also operate as a Peltier cooler by reversing the applied current.
method: The dynamics are analyzed using Langevin equations to model the superconducting phases under thermal fluctuations, and thermodynamic principles (First Law) are applied to calculate work and heat flow.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting circuit incorporating a Josephson junction-based diode, coupled to two thermal reservoirs at different temperatures ($T_1$ and $T_2$).
key_observables: Output power, efficiency ($\eta$), Seebeck coefficient ($S$), open-circuit voltage ($V_1$), work ($\dot{W}$), and heat flows ($\dot{Q}_1, \dot{Q}_2$).
important_parameters: Temperature gradient ($\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$), coupling strength ($\kappa$), and external bias current ($I_{	ext{ext}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a small effective inductance ($V_1 \approx V_2$) and focuses on the regime where work extraction is driven by thermal fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the efficiency ($\eta$) dependence on reservoir temperatures and coupling strength, and show the optimal conditions for maximum efficiency, confirming the heat engine and cooling capabilities.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and theoretical framework using Langevin equations. It then analyzes the heat engine performance by calculating work and efficiency, followed by an investigation of the reverse operation (Peltier cooling) using the Seebeck coefficient.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and energy conversion at the nanoscale, which is a key area connecting statistical mechanics to quantum phenomena and open quantum systems.

FIG. 2. Open-circuit voltage is shown in units of V0 = I0R, while the temperature T1 of the ‘cold’ reservoir is given in units of T0 = EJ/kB. The values of the ‘hot’ reservoir tem- perature T2 are indicated in the inset. The coupling strength is fixed at κ = ℏ2/(4e2EJLeff) = 0.1 for all curves. Panel (a) demonstrates that for T2 ≲2.3T0, the maximum voltage occurs at finite T1, whereas for T2 ≳2.3T0, the maximum is reached at T1 →0 [panel (b)]. The blue curve for T2 = 6T0 and T1 = 0 marks the overall maximum voltage V1 = 0.045V0 attainable at κ = 0.1.

FIG. 3. Open-circuit voltage is shown in units of V0 = RI0, and the cold-reservoir temperature T1 is given in units of T0 = EJ/kB. The values of the dimensionless coupling constant κ are indicated in the inset. The hot-reservoir temperature is fixed at T2 = 5T0 for all curves. Panel (a) shows that for κ ≲0.04, the maximum voltage occurs at finite T1, whereas for κ ≳0.04 the maximum shifts to T1 →0, see panel (b). For consistency, the case κ = 0 is also included, where the voltage vanishes as expected.

FIG. 4. (a) Circuit voltage in units of V0 = RI0 as a function of Iext in units of I0. The circuit parameters are κ = 0.1, T2 = 2.3T0 and T1 = 0. This panel demonstrates that the dependence of the voltage as a function of the external applied current is linear in our regime. The point of maximum power is given for the values of Iext in which the voltage takes half of its maximum value. (b) Heat flow when operated as a heat engine: the lower and upper branches of the circuit are presented respectively as hot and cold reservoirs. The circuit works as a heat engine, extracting the heat −Q2 from the hot reservoir, delivering Q1 to the cold reservoir while producing the work W = −Q1 −Q2.

At the same time, the tem- perature T2 at which the efficiency reaches its maximum shifts toward lower values.
